articles.title: Buying a Plot in Bengaluru: BDA, BMRDA and BIAAPA Approvals Explained
articles.excerpt: A site is only as good as the approval behind it. Who sanctions what around Bengaluru, what a release order is, why conversion matters, and the red flags that should end a conversation.
articles.content:
Buying a site is simpler than buying a flat in every way except one. There is no construction to monitor, no possession date to worry about and no association to inherit. What there is instead is a chain of approvals, and if one link in it is missing, there is usually no way to repair it afterwards.

This guide explains who approves what around Bengaluru, and what to ask for at each step.

Who sanctions what

Which authority sanctioned a layout depends on where it is, and the answer changes what you should check.

  • BDA. The development authority for the city’s own planning area, which both develops its own layouts and approves private ones inside its jurisdiction.
  • BMRDA. The metropolitan region authority, covering a much wider area around the city through its local planning authorities. A great deal of the plotted supply on the outer corridors is sanctioned this way.
  • BIAAPA. The planning authority for the area around the international airport, which is why it appears on almost every layout in the Devanahalli belt.
  • BBMP. The municipal body, which maintains the khata and collects property tax within its limits; outside them, a panchayat or another local body does.

A layout approval from the right authority for that location is the foundation. An approval from the wrong one, or a "sanction pending" claim, is not a foundation at all.

The documents to ask for, in order

  1. The layout approval, with the sanctioned plan showing your site number in the released portion.
  2. The conversion order, showing the land was converted from agricultural use, and covering the extent your site sits on.
  3. The release order, confirming your specific site is among those released for sale.
  4. The mother deed and the title chain, going back thirty years, with an encumbrance certificate for the same period.
  5. The khata for the site, and the tax paid receipts — our khata guide explains which register you want to be in and why.
  6. A current survey sketch, and ideally your own surveyor walking the site with it.

The municipal records for areas inside city limits are published at bbmp.gov.in; outside them, ask which local body maintains the record and check there.

Walk the site

Documents tell you what should be there. A visit tells you what is.

  • Are the corner stones in place and does the site match the sketch?
  • Are the roads formed and blacktopped, or marked on a plan and nothing else?
  • Are the storm-water drains cut, and does the ground fall away from your site or towards it?
  • Is there a transformer, are the street lights in, and is there a water line?
  • What is on the adjoining sites — built houses, or scrub?

A layout where the infrastructure went in before the sales started is a layout whose developer had the money to do it properly. That single observation tells you a great deal.

What a plot costs beyond the price

Sites look simpler than flats on the cost side, and they are, but there are still line items people forget. Stamp duty and registration apply as they do to any property. Fencing and a gate are the first thing you will spend on. Property tax runs from the year you register, built or not. And if you intend to build, the plan sanction, the deposits for water and power, and the compound wall all arrive before the first course of brickwork.

The other cost is time. A site that sits idle for a decade has cost you whatever that money would otherwise have earned, and unlike a flat it has produced no rent in the meantime. That is the trade a plot buyer is making, and it is worth making deliberately.

Red flags that should end the conversation

"Approval is in process." Buy approved land, or buy nothing.

A price well below the surrounding band. There is always a reason, and it is usually in the title, the conversion or the release.

Pressure to pay an advance to "hold" a site before you have seen the approval documents.

A seller who will only show photocopies. Originals are inspected at your lawyer’s office, not described over the phone.

Encroachment, a drain, or a high-tension line across the site. All three are visible on a visit and invisible in a brochure.

After you buy

Get the khata transferred into your name, pay the property tax annually even though nothing is built, and fence the site. An unfenced, untaxed site with a khata in somebody else’s name is the easiest property in the city to have a dispute about.

If you intend to build, check the layout bye-laws for setbacks and height before you commission a design, and read our north corridor guide if the site is in the Devanahalli belt.

One last habit worth forming: visit the site once a year even while it sits idle, and photograph the boundary stones. Encroachment on an unvisited plot starts small, with a neighbour’s wall a foot over the line, and it is far easier to raise in the first month than in the fifth year. A site is a low-maintenance asset, not a no-maintenance one.

faqs.question: What is a release order?
faqs.answer: An approved layout hands over a share of the sites to the developer for sale, in phases, by a release order. A site that has not been released is not a site you can safely register, whatever the brochure says.

faqs.question: What does conversion mean?
faqs.answer: Agricultural land has to be converted for non-agricultural use before it can be laid out for housing. The conversion carries an order, with a number. Ask for it, and check that the extent it covers includes your site.

faqs.question: Is a plot safer than an apartment?
faqs.answer: Different risks. A plot removes construction risk and adds approval risk: there is no builder to chase, but a defective approval is very hard to cure. Diligence on a plot is mostly documentary.

articles.title: Under-construction vs Ready-to-move: Which Should You Choose?
articles.excerpt: The two are priced differently because they carry different risks. A plain comparison of cost, timing, tax treatment, loan mechanics and what each one demands of a buyer.
articles.content:
This is the first real decision most buyers make, and it is usually made on price alone. The price difference is the easy part; what it is compensating you for is the part worth understanding.

The comparison, plainly

Under-constructionReady-to-move
PriceLower at launch, rising towards completionFull price, no further upside from the build
RiskDelivery, delay, specification changesWhat you see is what you buy
PaymentStaged against construction milestonesLargely at registration
While you waitRent and loan interest togetherNeither
ChoiceFloor, facing and unit still openWhatever is left unsold or on resale
VerificationDocuments, approvals, the developer’s recordThe building itself, and the association

The case for under-construction

You pay less, you choose the floor and the facing, and the payment is spread over the build rather than demanded at once. On a project that is delivered on time and to specification, the buyer who came in early is straightforwardly better off.

The conditions attached to that sentence are doing a lot of work. "Delivered on time" and "to specification" are the two things you cannot verify in advance, which is why the diligence on an under-construction purchase is documentary: the registration record, the approvals, the developer’s delivery history, the escrow arrangement. Our RERA guide lists what to read and where.

The case for ready-to-move

You see the actual flat, the actual light at the actual time of day, the actual water pressure and the actual neighbours. You stop paying rent the month you move in. There is no delivery risk, because delivery has happened.

What you give up is the discount and the choice. Ready inventory is what did not sell, or what somebody is reselling, which means the floor and facing are given rather than chosen. You are also inheriting a building with a history — so the diligence shifts from documents to the fabric: the association accounts, the sinking fund, the last three years of repairs, and what the residents say when you ask them in the lift.

The money, side by side

Three differences matter and they compound.

  1. Double outflow. During construction you pay rent and loan interest at the same time. On a three-year build that is a real number, and it eats a good part of the discount.
  2. Staged disbursal. Interest accrues only on what has been drawn, which helps early and matters less as the draws add up. See our home loan guide.
  3. Tax treatment. An under-construction purchase and a completed one are treated differently for indirect tax, and the deduction position on interest paid during construction has its own rules. Both change from time to time — confirm the current position with your accountant rather than with a brochure.

Verifying an under-construction project

The diligence here is almost entirely documentary, and it is the same list every time: the registration record and its quarterly updates, the sanctioned plan, the title to the land, the approvals, and the developer’s record on their last three completed projects. That last item is the most predictive and the most often skipped — go and look at a building they finished four years ago, and talk to somebody who lives in it.

Ask also for the specification in writing. A brochure that promises imported marble and an agreement that says vitrified tiles or equivalent are not the same promise, and it is the agreement that governs.

Verifying a ready-to-move property

Here the building answers most of the questions, if you look properly. Walk the basement and the terrace. Read the association’s accounts for the last three years and ask what the sinking fund holds. Find out what the last major repair cost and how it was funded. Check the occupancy certificate exists, and check the water arrangement in summer rather than in December.

Then check the one thing a resale buyer inherits that a new buyer does not: the undivided share of land recorded in the deed, and whether the khata for the individual flat has been issued.

What we tell clients

If you are renting and your budget is tight, ready-to-move almost always wins, because the double outflow is the thing that breaks household budgets. If you have somewhere to live, a horizon of three years and the stomach for the diligence, under-construction in a credible project is a reasonable trade.

One more consideration that rarely makes the comparison tables: what the two options do to your flexibility. A ready flat can be let from the month you take possession, which turns a purchase into an income-producing asset immediately if your plans change. An under-construction unit cannot be let, cannot easily be sold before completion in a slow market, and ties up money for years in something that does not yet exist.

And if you are on the fence, look at both in the same week. A show flat and a lived-in flat feel completely different, and the difference will tell you more about your own preference than any table will. Start with our ready-to-move listings and compare them against a launch on the same corridor — the state portal at rera.karnataka.gov.in will tell you what the launch has actually declared.

faqs.question: Is under-construction always cheaper?
faqs.answer: At launch, usually. The gap narrows as the building goes up, and by the time it is complete it has generally closed. What you are buying with the discount is time and risk, not a bargain.

faqs.question: What happens to my EMI while the flat is being built?
faqs.answer: The lender disburses in stages against the builder’s demands, and you pay interest on what has been disbursed until the loan is fully drawn. If you are also paying rent, budget for both at once.

faqs.question: Which is better for a first home?
faqs.answer: For most first-time buyers who are currently renting, ready-to-move, because it removes the double outflow and the delivery risk. Under-construction rewards buyers with time, tolerance and a lawyer.

articles.title: First-time Homebuyer Checklist for Bengaluru
articles.excerpt: Everything a first-time buyer in Bengaluru should do, in the order it should be done: budget, pre-approval, shortlist, visits, diligence, negotiation, registration and the month after.
articles.content:
Buying your first home in Bengaluru is a sequence, and most of the expensive mistakes come from doing the steps out of order — falling in love with a flat before knowing the budget, paying a booking amount before a title check, arranging the loan after agreeing a price. This is the order we recommend.

1. Work out the real budget

Not the price you can imagine paying: the total you can actually fund. That means the down payment, the loan you qualify for, the stamp duty and registration, the brokerage, and a fit-out reserve. Our stamp duty guide covers the closing costs, which are the line people most often leave out.

A budget that does not include the closing costs is not a budget. It is a hope with a number attached.

2. Get a pre-approval

Before you look. It converts a guess into a number, it surfaces any credit-report problem while you still have time to fix it, and it makes you a more credible buyer. Our home loan guide explains what the lender is actually computing.

3. Define the brief before the shortlist

Four things, written down: the localities you will consider, the configuration, the maximum all-in price, and the timeline. A brief that says "anywhere in east Bengaluru, two or three bedrooms, around a crore, sometime this year" will produce forty viewings and no decision.

4. Shortlist, then visit properly

  • Visit at the hour you would actually commute, not at a convenient hour on a Sunday.
  • See the actual unit, not the show flat, and stand in it for ten minutes without talking.
  • Check water pressure, mobile signal, the lift, and what the parking bay is really sized for.
  • Ask a resident — not the sales team — what the maintenance bill is and what the last big repair was.
  • Look at the building’s worst corner: the basement, the terrace, the rear service passage.

5. Do the diligence before the money

  1. Title chain and encumbrance certificate, checked by your own lawyer.
  2. Khata and tax paid receipts — which register, in whose name.
  3. Approved plan, commencement and, for a completed building, the occupancy certificate.
  4. For an under-construction project, the record on the state portal at rera.karnataka.gov.in.
  5. For a resale flat, the association no-dues and the undivided land share in the deed.

None of this is optional and none of it is expensive relative to the transaction. The lawyer’s fee is the cheapest insurance in the process.

6. Negotiate on the whole package

Price is one variable. Others that move more easily: the floor, the parking bay, the payment schedule, who pays the brokerage, what the seller leaves behind, and the date of handover. A seller who will not move on price will often move on three of those.

7. Register, and then finish the job

Registration is not the end. Afterwards: transfer the khata into your name, get the electricity and water connections changed over, register with the association, and keep the registered deed, the challan and the receipts together in one place. Our khata guide explains why the transfer should not wait.

8. The month after

Budget for it. The first month of a new home always costs more than expected — fittings, curtains, a plumber, a deposit for something. A small reserve makes the difference between settling in and starting the first year anxious about money.

Two mistakes that cost the most

Stretching the budget because of one feature. A larger balcony, a nicer lobby or a marginally better view will not feel worth the extra in the third year of the loan. Decide the ceiling before you fall for something, and hold it.

Paying anything before the documents are read. A booking amount is the moment your negotiating position weakens, and it is almost always paid before the title check because the sales team creates urgency. There is always another flat. There is rarely another chance to unwind a payment cleanly.

What nobody tells first-time buyers

Three things worth knowing in advance. The process will take longer than anybody promises, and the delay is usually in documentation rather than in decisions. You will be asked for the same set of papers by three different parties, so scan everything once and keep it in one folder. And the flat that feels right on the second visit usually still feels right on the fifth — the visit that changes your mind is the one where you go alone, at a different hour, and simply stand there.

The shortest version

Know the total budget. Get pre-approved. Write the brief. See ten properties, not forty. Let a lawyer read the papers before you pay anything. Negotiate on more than price. Finish the paperwork after registration rather than a year later. If you would like help with any of it, an advisor can take the first three steps with you — and you can start browsing ready-to-move homes whenever you are ready.

faqs.question: How much should I keep aside beyond the price?
faqs.answer: Enough for stamp duty, registration, brokerage, the portion the lender will not fund, and the first round of fit-out. Treat it as a separate budget line, because none of it can be deferred.

faqs.question: Should I get a loan pre-approval before shortlisting?
faqs.answer: Yes. A pre-approval tells you your actual budget rather than your hoped-for one, and it makes your offer stronger with a seller who has been let down before.

faqs.question: How many properties should I see?
faqs.answer: Enough to calibrate, which for most buyers is six to ten inside a defined budget and locality. Seeing thirty across four corridors usually means the brief is not defined yet.

faqs.question: How do I start a property search with Squares N Acres?
faqs.answer: Tell us the locality, the budget and the configuration you have in mind through any enquiry form on the site. An advisor comes back with a shortlist drawn from our own inventory, explains where each option is weak as well as strong, and arranges the site visits.

faqs.question: Do you charge the buyer a fee?
faqs.answer: Our commercial terms depend on the transaction and are agreed in writing before you commit to anything. Ask the advisor for the terms at the first conversation rather than at the offer stage — a brokerage that will not put its fee in writing is telling you something.

faqs.question: What documents should I check before paying a booking amount?
faqs.answer: At a minimum: the title deeds for the last thirty years, the approved plan, the commencement certificate, the khata and the latest tax paid receipt, the encumbrance certificate, and the RERA registration where the project needs one. For a resale flat, add the society or association no-dues certificate and the share of undivided land recorded in the sale deed.

faqs.question: How do you price a property for sale?
faqs.answer: From three things: what comparable units in the same building or layout have actually transacted at, what is currently listed and not selling, and the condition and floor of your specific unit. We will tell you when a price you have in mind is unlikely to transact, which is the useful part of the exercise.

faqs.question: What does listing with you involve?
faqs.answer: A visit to photograph and measure the property, a documentation check so that questions are answered before a buyer asks them, a listing on this site, and screened viewings. You keep the decision on every offer; we handle the negotiation and the paperwork that follows it.

faqs.question: How much deposit is normal for a rental in Bengaluru?
faqs.answer: Deposits in the city have historically been high by Indian standards — several months of rent is common, and the exact figure is negotiable rather than fixed. Agree the deposit, the notice period and the lock-in together, because owners often trade one against another.

faqs.question: Who pays for maintenance in a rented flat?
faqs.answer: Say so in the agreement rather than assuming. The usual split is that the owner pays the association maintenance and the structural repairs, and the tenant pays the utilities and anything they break. Fixtures that fail through age are the owner’s; fixtures that fail through use are argued about, so write them down.

faqs.question: Is a rental agreement required to be registered?
faqs.answer: Short agreements are commonly executed on stamp paper and notarised, while longer tenures attract registration. The threshold and the stamp duty payable are set by state rules that change, so confirm the current position with the sub-registrar office or your lawyer before signing.

faqs.question: How much home loan am I eligible for?
faqs.answer: Most lenders work backwards from your income: they cap the total of all your monthly obligations at a share of your net income, then convert what is left into a loan at the current rate and tenure. Your credit history, the co-applicant’s income and the property’s valuation all move the number. Our home-loan page has a calculator that shows the arithmetic.

faqs.question: Should I take a fixed or a floating rate?
faqs.answer: Floating rates in India are usually linked to an external benchmark, which means they move with it in both directions; fixed rates buy certainty at a premium and often convert to floating after a few years. Read which benchmark the loan is tied to and how often it resets — that detail matters more than the headline rate.

faqs.question: What does the bank need from the builder before it releases money?
faqs.answer: For an under-construction purchase the lender needs the project’s legal and technical clearance, and then releases money in stages against the builder’s demand letters and the construction progress. Ask whether your project is already on the lender’s approved list — it shortens the process considerably.

faqs.question: What is the difference between A khata and B khata?
faqs.answer: A khata records a property as fully compliant with the municipal body’s requirements; a B khata records one that is on the tax rolls but does not meet them. The practical difference shows up when you need a building plan approval, a trade licence or a home loan. Our guide on the subject sets out what can and cannot be converted.

faqs.question: How long should a title search go back?
faqs.answer: Thirty years is the convention in Karnataka, together with an encumbrance certificate covering the same period. If the chain passes through an inheritance, a partition or a power of attorney, ask your lawyer to look further rather than treating the thirty years as a rule.

faqs.question: Does every project have to be registered under RERA?
faqs.answer: Registration applies to projects above the thresholds the Act sets for land area and number of units. Smaller developments, and projects already complete when the Act came into force, can fall outside it. Check the project on the Karnataka RERA portal rather than taking a brochure’s word for it.

faqs.question: What does a RERA registration number actually tell me?
faqs.answer: That the promoter has declared the project’s land title, approvals, plans, unit inventory and completion date on a public record, and that changes to those declarations leave a trail. It is not a quality certificate and it is not a guarantee of delivery — it is a record you can hold the promoter to.

faqs.question: Where do I complain if a project is delayed?
faqs.answer: Complaints against a registered project go to the state authority, with the appellate tribunal above it. Keep every payment receipt, the allotment letter and the agreement to sale: a complaint stands or falls on the paper trail, not on the correspondence.

faqs.question: Can an NRI buy property in Bengaluru?
faqs.answer: Non-resident Indians and persons of Indian origin may generally buy residential and commercial property in India, with agricultural land, plantations and farmhouses treated differently. Payment must come through banking channels from an appropriate account. Confirm the current exchange-control position with your bank before you remit anything.

faqs.question: Do I need to be in India to complete a purchase?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. A properly executed power of attorney lets somebody register on your behalf, but it has to be drafted for the specific transaction and attested correctly in the country you are in. Arrange it early: getting the attestation right takes longer than the registration itself.

faqs.question: Are the listings on this site verified?
faqs.answer: We visit what we list and check the areas, the approvals and the charges before publishing, and we correct a listing when something changes. That is a different claim from "guaranteed": your own legal due diligence still belongs in the process, and we will tell you what to look at.

faqs.question: Which parts of Bengaluru do you cover?
faqs.answer: Twenty localities across the north, south, east, west and centre of the city, listed on the localities page. We work one city properly rather than several superficially, which is what makes the locality advice worth reading.

items.title: Title verification
items.summary: Thirty years of title, read properly.
items.html:
We trace the chain of ownership for the conventional thirty-year period, read the encumbrance certificate for the same window, and flag anything that needs a further look — an inheritance, a partition, a power of attorney in the chain.

The output is a written opinion you can act on, not a verbal assurance.

items.title: Agreement drafting
items.summary: Agreements that say what was actually agreed.
items.html:
Sale agreements, agreements to sale, rental and lease agreements, and joint development agreements, drafted or reviewed so that the commercial terms you negotiated are the terms in the document.

We pay particular attention to the schedule of the property, the payment milestones and the consequences of a delay on either side.

items.title: RERA compliance
items.summary: Reading the project record, and acting on it.
items.html:
We check the project’s registration and its declarations, compare them with what you have been offered, and raise the discrepancies before you pay.

Where a complaint is warranted, we help assemble the paper trail the authority will actually decide on.

items.title: Property registration
items.summary: Duty, appointment, execution and the khata that follows.
items.html: Computation of duty and fees, the appointment, the execution at the sub-registrar’s office, and the khata transfer afterwards — which is the step most buyers postpone and then need urgently.

items.title: Due diligence
items.html:
A single report covering the approvals, the conversion where land is involved, the khata and tax position, encumbrances, and any litigation touching the property or the promoter.

For a plot, this is most of the transaction.

items.title: Dispute resolution
items.summary: When something has already gone wrong.
items.html: Delayed possession, a builder who will not hand over the documents, a boundary dispute, a society that will not issue a no-dues certificate. We advise on the forum, the evidence and the realistic outcome before you spend on litigation.

data.title: Real estate awareness
data.subtitle: The things everybody assumes you already know, set out plainly — and a short quiz to find out whether you do.

items.label: A large share of what a promoter collects for a registered project must sit in a separate project account — verify the current share with the authority.
Units in registered projects are sold on carpet area, which is smaller than the super built-up area in the brochure — verify both before you compare prices.
The conventional period a title search covers in Karnataka, with an encumbrance certificate for the same window — verify with your lawyer.
Stamp duty is assessed on the guidance value or the consideration, whichever is higher — verify the current value for the locality.
Principal repayment on a home loan falls within an overall annual deduction limit shared with other investments — verify the current limit with your accountant.
A property on the B register can be taxed but generally cannot get a building plan approval — verify the current position with the municipal body.

items.title: RERA
items.summary: What registration puts on the public record.
items.html:
A registered project declares its land title, approvals, plans, unit inventory and completion date publicly, and files progress updates. That record is what you can hold a promoter to. It is not a quality certificate.

Read the full guide: Karnataka RERA for homebuyers.

items.title: Registration
items.summary: What happens at the sub-registrar’s office.
items.html:
Duty and fees are computed and paid, an appointment is booked, both parties attend with witnesses, and the deed is executed and recorded. The khata transfer is a separate application afterwards.

Read the full guide: stamp duty and registration charges.

items.title: Home loans
items.summary: How a lender decides what you can borrow.
items.html:
Income minus existing obligations, capped as a ratio, converted into a loan at the current rate and tenure, and limited by a loan-to-value cap on the property’s assessed value.

Read the full guide: home loan eligibility and FOIR.

items.title: Tax benefits
items.html:
Interest and principal on a home loan attract deductions under different sections, with separate limits and conditions, and the treatment differs for a self-occupied and a let property.

The limits are revised periodically — confirm the current position with your accountant rather than with an article.

items.title: Stamp duty
items.summary: A tax on the instrument, not on the deal.
items.html:
Assessed on the higher of the guidance value and the consideration, with registration fees and cess on top. Rates and concessions are set by the state and revised from time to time.

Verify the current rates on the state’s registration portal before you budget.

items.title: Documents checklist
items.html:
Title chain and encumbrance certificate, khata and tax receipts, approved plan and commencement certificate, occupancy certificate for a completed building, and the association no-dues for a resale flat.

The khata is the one buyers most often get wrong: A khata and B khata explained.

data.title: How much do you actually know?
data.intro: Five questions. The explanations matter more than the score.

questions.question: What does a khata prove?
options: That the municipality holds you liable for the property tax
That the building plan was approved
That the property has no encumbrance
questions.explanation: A khata is a municipal record of tax liability. Ownership comes from the registered deed and the title chain.

questions.question: Stamp duty is calculated on…
options: The price stated in the deed, always
Whichever of the two is higher
questions.explanation: Duty is assessed on the higher of the consideration and the published guidance value, which is why buying below guidance value does not reduce it.

questions.question: A RERA registration number tells you that…
options: The construction quality has been inspected
The project will be delivered on time
The project’s declarations are on a public record
questions.explanation: Registration puts declarations on the record and makes changes traceable. It certifies nothing about quality, delivery or finances.

questions.question: Which area figure must a registered project state in the agreement?
questions.explanation: The Act defines carpet area and requires units to be sold on it, which is what makes two projects comparable.

questions.question: What most often decides your home loan amount?
questions.explanation: Lenders cap the share of net income that goes to committed payments. That ratio, not the property price, usually sets the ceiling.

data.title: Before you pay anything
data.intro: Ten things to have done, or to have somebody do for you.

items.text: Read the project or property record on the state portal
items.detail: For a registered project, end to end, including the updates.

items.text: Get the title chain checked for thirty years
items.detail: By your own lawyer, not the seller’s.

items.text: Pull the encumbrance certificate yourself
items.detail: For the same period as the title search.

items.text: Check the khata and which register it sits in
items.detail: And that the name matches the deed exactly.

items.text: Collect the property tax paid receipts
items.detail: For the last several years, with no gaps.

items.text: See the approved plan and the commencement certificate
items.detail: And check the block you were shown is on it.

items.text: Ask for the occupancy certificate
Get the carpet area in writing
items.detail: Alongside the super built-up area you were quoted.

items.text: Confirm where your payments go
items.detail: The account named in the agreement, never cash.

items.text: Budget the closing costs separately
items.detail: Stamp duty, registration and charges are payable on the day.

jobOpenings.title: Real Estate Advisor — Bengaluru
jobOpenings.description:
We are looking for an advisor to work with buyers across Bengaluru: understanding a requirement properly, shortlisting from our own inventory, running site visits, and staying with the client through negotiation and registration.

You will own your files end to end. Nobody will hand your client to a different desk halfway through, and nobody will ask you to sell something you would not buy.

This is a placeholder job record created for the seed. Replace the description, the responsibilities, the requirements and the compensation with the client’s own before the careers page goes live.
responsibilities: Qualify incoming enquiries and understand each buyer’s requirement in detail
Shortlist properties from the curated inventory and arrange site visits
Attend visits, and set out honestly what is weak about each option as well as what is strong
Maintain accurate records of every interaction in the admin panel
Coordinate with developers, lenders and legal advisers through the transaction
requirements: Two to five years in residential real estate or a comparable consultative sales role
Working knowledge of Bengaluru’s residential micro-markets
Fluency in English and Kannada; a third language is an advantage
A two-wheeler or car and a valid driving licence for site visits
Comfort with a CRM and with writing things down

jobOpenings.title: Digital Marketing Specialist
jobOpenings.description:
We are looking for somebody to own how this site is found: search, content distribution, paid campaigns and the measurement behind all three.

The SEO side of the role is substantial. The site is built around a structured content model and an SEO manager, and the person in this role decides what gets written and how it is targeted.

responsibilities: Own organic search performance: keyword research, on-page work and content briefs
Plan and run paid campaigns across search and social, against a defined cost per lead
Work with the editorial desks on the article pipeline and the locality pages
Report on traffic, lead quality and cost per qualified lead every month
Keep the analytics and tracking setup honest and documented
requirements: Three to six years in digital marketing, with real ownership of an organic search programme
Hands-on with analytics, search console and a campaign platform
Able to write a content brief that a subject-matter writer can work from
Comfortable being measured on qualified leads rather than on impressions

jobOpenings.title: Property Analyst
jobOpenings.description:
We are looking for an analyst to keep our locality data, price bands and yield estimates current, and to write the market pieces that come out of them.

This is a research role with a publishing output. Half the week is data — transactions, supply, absorption, rents — and half is turning it into something a buyer can act on.

responsibilities: Track supply, pricing and absorption across the localities we cover
Maintain the locality price bands and the indicative yield estimates
Write market pieces and comparisons for the insights section
Support advisors with valuation comparables on live transactions
Flag when a published figure has gone stale
requirements: One to four years in real estate research, valuation, or a data-led analyst role
Strong spreadsheet skills and a healthy scepticism about sources
Able to write clearly for a non-specialist reader
Knowledge of Bengaluru’s geography, or the willingness to learn it properly

jobOpenings.title: Customer Relations Manager (Part-time)
jobOpenings.description:
We are looking for somebody part-time to look after clients between the milestones: after a site visit, during a loan application, and in the weeks around registration.

The role exists because the gaps are where clients feel abandoned. Twenty to twenty-five hours a week, with the timing arranged around school hours if that suits.

Track documentation status across live transactions and chase what is missing
Collect feedback after every completed transaction and log it honestly
Keep the CRM accurate, which is most of what makes the rest possible
requirements: Two to four years in client servicing, operations or customer success
Unusually good written communication in English; Kannada or Hindi an advantage
